messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Dream Residue: Waking up from a nightmare, Olfactory (Cologne/Perfume): A specific perfume or cologne, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Open Spaces: Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
  Memory: Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

Vignette:
Layla was thirty-one when the convoy she was driving in was hit by an improvised explosive device on a road just outside Mosul. She remembers the dust, the silence after the blast, and then the shouting. What she cannot remember, no matter how many times she has tried, is the moment of impact itself. There is a gap in the film of her mind, a skip, and then she is on the ground, ears ringing, watching the translator—a quiet man named Khalid who always wore a faint spicy cologne—slumped against the Humvee door, not moving. She has never been able to piece together the seconds between the noise and the stillness. The memories come in fragments: the smell of diesel and copper, the heat, the weight of her weapon, but never in the right order, never forming a whole story.

For the past fourteen years, Layla has lived with those fragments. She is an auditor now, working for a state agency in a glass-and-steel office building downtown. The open-plan floor makes her skin crawl. Every morning she walks the long way to her cubicle, hugging the wall, scanning each face, noting every exit. She has memorized the building's stairwells and fire doors. She never sits with her back to the room. Colleagues have joked about her being paranoid; she has learned to smile and say she likes to see who's coming.

The worst moments come without warning. A coworker's perfume—something floral with a warm base note—can flood her with a panic so immediate she has to excuse herself to the restroom and stand with her hands gripping the sink until her breathing slows. Khalid's cologne was like that, she thinks, though she cannot be certain. Every sudden bang—a filing cabinet slamming, a car backfiring in the street—sends her heart into her throat and her gaze darting to the nearest cover. She knows these reactions make no sense in a suburban office park, but her body does not seem to care what she knows. It acts as if the danger is still there, as if she is still the person who could not protect the people around her.

That belief has taken root deeply. Layla is convinced that the attack happened because of who she is—a woman, an Arab who chose to serve, someone who was not strong enough or quick enough. She replays counterfactual scenarios constantly: if she had taken a different route, if she had stopped to check the road, if she had been more alert, Khalid would still be alive. The marriage she had before the deployment ended a few years after she came home. Her husband could not understand why she needed the bedroom door locked, why she jumped at his footsteps, why she could not sit in the backyard without her shoulders tensed. They tried counseling, but she could not explain the gaps in her memory, the way the story would not hold together long enough for her to tell it.

She has built a narrow life that feels manageable. She lives alone in a small apartment with a deadbolt and a chain lock. There are exactly three places where she feels safe: her bedroom, her bathroom with the door closed, and her car with all doors locked. Everywhere else requires vigilance. She checks behind her on the street, identifies escape routes in grocery stores and waiting rooms, avoids open plazas and parking lots where there is nowhere to hide. The consequence has been a slow shrinking of her world. She no longer visits her sister, who lives in a house with large windows and an open front yard. She has turned down promotions that would require travel to new cities. She is reliable at her desk work but has no close colleagues, no after-work drinks, no one who knows what she does when the lights are off and the dream residue of a nightmare leaves her gasping at 3 a.m., the ghost of Khalid's cologne still in her nostrils.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning two weeks ago, when a loud truck backfired outside her office. She dropped to the floor, halfway under her desk, hands over her head, and stayed there for several moments before she realized what she had done. A security guard came over; she said she had tripped. That evening, sitting in her locked apartment, she understood that the fragments were not going to sort themselves out, that her body would keep reacting as if the convoy were still burning, and that she was tired of living inside what she could not piece together. She is afraid of what she might find if she looks at the gaps too closely, but she is even more afraid of spending another decade hiding from a smell she cannot forget.
